"Awkward" describes anything that doesn't fit smoothly or comfortably — a clumsy movement, an embarrassing social moment, a hard-to-handle object, an inconvenient time, or a person who doesn't quite know how to act. The feeling the word carries is one of something being slightly off, out of place, or not working the way it naturally should. Think of it as the opposite of smooth, easy, and natural.
1. Physically clumsy or ungraceful

When a person moves or performs an action without grace or coordination, we call it awkward. An awkward walk looks stiff or unbalanced. An awkward attempt to catch a ball looks clumsy and uncertain. An awkward wave goodbye might be a stiff, strange gesture that somehow doesn't look right.

The key idea is that the movement draws attention to itself precisely because it lacks the natural, smooth quality you'd expect. "He made an awkward jump and landed badly." "She gave an awkward smile — like she was forcing it."
2. Socially uncomfortable situations

This is probably the most common modern use. A situation, conversation, or moment is awkward when it makes the people involved feel uncomfortable, embarrassed, or unsure of what to say or do.

The classic "awkward silence" is when nobody speaks, and instead of feeling peaceful, it feels tense — like everyone is waiting for someone to say something but no one does. A first date with no chemistry is awkward. Running into an ex at a party is awkward. Saying something offensive by accident in front of a group and watching everyone go quiet — that's deeply awkward.

These situations feel awkward because of a mismatch: conversations are supposed to flow, social gatherings are supposed to have a comfortable energy, and when they don't, something feels wrong. "There was an awkward pause after she made the joke and nobody laughed." "He brought up money at the dinner table, and the whole room went silent. Very awkward."
3. Feeling awkward personally

A person can feel awkward as an internal emotion — meaning they feel self-conscious, out of place, or unsure of how to behave, even if nobody else around them feels the same way.

You might feel awkward at a formal party where you don't know anyone. You might feel awkward giving a speech if you're shy. You might feel awkward telling someone bad news. In each case, you feel uncertain and like you don't quite belong in the moment. "I always feel awkward when I have to speak in public." "She felt awkward being the only person who didn't know anyone."
4. A person who is socially awkward

When we describe someone as awkward — or "socially awkward" — we mean they generally struggle to handle social situations comfortably. They might say the wrong thing at the wrong time, not know when to stop talking, miss social cues, or simply seem uncomfortable around people.

It's worth knowing that being socially awkward is not inherently a flaw in character. Many people who are awkward are also kind, intelligent, and interesting. The word just describes the fact that social interaction doesn't come naturally to them. "He's a brilliant scientist but terribly awkward at parties." "She's a bit awkward at first, but once you get to know her, she's wonderful."
5. Difficult to use, handle, or move

An object can be awkward if it's hard to use or handle — usually because of its shape, size, weight, or position. This has nothing to do with emotions; it's purely about physical inconvenience.

"The sofa was an awkward shape and barely fit through the door." "Carrying three large bags at once is awkward." "The shelf is in an awkward spot — you keep hitting your head on it."

A task or problem can also be awkward when it's difficult to deal with — especially when there's no clean or easy solution. "Being asked to take sides in a fight between two close friends is an awkward position to be in."
6. Inconvenient timing

Something can be described as awkward if it happens at a time that is inconvenient or poorly chosen. "Could we reschedule? Three in the morning is an awkward time for a call." "You've caught me at an awkward moment — can I call you back in ten minutes?"
7. Being deliberately difficult (especially British English)

In British English particularly, if someone is "being awkward," it means they are deliberately uncooperative, stubborn, or obstructive — making things harder than they need to be on purpose. "Don't be awkward — just sign the form." "He's being awkward about returning the money."
The one big idea behind all the meanings

Look across all these uses and you'll notice one unifying thread: something that should flow or fit naturally doesn't. A movement lacks grace. A conversation lacks ease. An object lacks the right shape for the task. A time lacks convenience. A person lacks social comfort. In every case, "awkward" is pointing to that gap between how something should go and how it's actually going.
How it compares to similar words

Clumsy focuses specifically on lack of physical coordination — a clumsy person trips, drops things, and breaks things. "Awkward" is broader and covers social and situational difficulty too.

Embarrassing focuses on the emotion of embarrassment. An awkward moment is often embarrassing, but "awkward" also captures the tension of the situation itself, not just how someone feels about it.

Uncomfortable describes general discomfort. "Awkward" implies a more specific quality — the sense that something is out of place or doesn't fit, which is what causes the discomfort.

Inconvenient is the closest word to the "bad timing" sense of awkward, but "awkward" is softer and more conversational.
Common phrases to know

"An awkward silence" — a pause in conversation that feels tense rather than comfortable. "An awkward moment" — a brief, uncomfortable situation, usually social. "Put someone in an awkward position" — to place someone in a situation where any choice they make is difficult or uncomfortable. "Feel awkward" — to feel self-conscious or out of place. "A bit awkward" vs "terribly awkward" — you can use degree words freely with this adjective; the stronger the word, the worse the situation.
The related forms

Awkwardly (adverb): describes how something is done — "He laughed awkwardly." Awkwardness (noun): the state or quality of being awkward — "The awkwardness in the room was obvious."

In short, whenever you encounter "awkward," ask yourself: what is it that doesn't fit smoothly here? The answer will always point you to the right meaning.
